goal/goal: The goal: turn a color image, thirty two by thirty two pixels, into ten class scores, one per class.
goal/linear: A linear classifier does it in one step, with a weight for every pixel, so what it learns is tied to places: move the cat's ear a few pixels, and different weights see it.
goal/conv: A convolution slides one small filter over the whole image, so it finds its pattern wherever it sits.
goal/relu: A ReLU bends the result, so stacked layers do not collapse into one linear step.
goal/pool: Pooling shrinks each map, keeping the strongest response in each window.
goal/name: Stack those a few times, then score what is left with a linear classifier, and you have a convolutional network: a ConvNet, for short.
goal/lenet: The shape is old. In 1998, Yann LeCun and colleagues described Le Net five: convolutions, each followed by a small averaging pool, then fully connected layers giving ten outputs, one per digit. Networks like it read millions of bank checks a day.
stages/input: Follow the shape through. The image is three by thirty two by thirty two: three color channels first, then height and width.
stages/conv: The first conv has sixteen filters, so it makes sixteen channels.
stages/pad: Its filters are three by three, and padding one gives back the two positions such a filter loses, so the grid stays put: sixteen by thirty two by thirty two.
stages/relu: The ReLU bends each entry on its own, so the shape does not change.
stages/pool: Two by two max pooling halves the height and the width: sixteen by sixteen by sixteen. Conv, ReLU, pool: that is one stage.
stages/nopad: Without padding, the conv would shrink it first: thirty two, minus three, plus one, is thirty, pooled to fifteen.
stages/repeat: A second stage, with thirty two filters, makes thirty two channels and pools them to eight by eight: thirty two by eight by eight.
stages/deeper: Each channel maps where one pattern shows up. Stage by stage, the block gets smaller and deeper: fewer positions, more patterns.
head/flatten: A linear classifier needs one vector, so flatten lays every number out in a row: thirty two times eight times eight, two thousand and forty eight.
head/fc: Then a fully connected layer: each of the ten scores has its own weight for every one of those numbers, plus a bias. Exactly a linear classifier.
head/names: PyTorch calls it n n dot linear: a linear layer and a fully connected layer are the same thing.
head/order: So the order follows the shapes. Convs and pools work on grids, so they come first; flatten makes the vector the linear layer scores.
count/one: Now count what it learns. A first-layer filter is three by three over three channels, twenty seven weights, plus one bias: twenty eight.
count/c1: Sixteen filters make four hundred and forty eight.
count/c2: The second conv's thirty two filters, each sixteen channels deep, hold four thousand, six hundred and forty, counted the same way.
count/lin: The linear layer has two thousand and forty eight weights for each of ten scores, plus ten biases: twenty thousand, four hundred and ninety.
count/most: ReLU and pooling learn nothing. Of the twenty five thousand, five hundred and seventy eight in all, four fifths sit in that last layer.
count/alexnet: Big networks lean the same way. AlexNet, in 2012, was this recipe at scale: five conv layers, three fully connected, sixty million parameters, and no conv layer held more than one percent of them.
